text_blocks.text: So right there, she's trying, I think. I mean, she could have been more assertive. Judge Mills -- so your opening, like, was -- was forceful. Judge Mills is a very experienced district judge. He had been a former Mississippi Supreme Court justice. He knows what he's doing. He read the record entirely differently than you did, and he pointed to this -- this -- this part right here where she's trying, I think -- we weren't there; we don't have an audio recording -- to -- to make the objections, and -- and the court says, "you already made those," they're clear, and "the court finds there to be no Batson violation." I don't know, at that point, she could have said, well, you're wrong, Judge. I get that. And Justice Alito has a good -- good points on that. But it seems pretty clear at that point.

Well, Your Honor, she preserved her objection. She didn't preserve the pretext arguments, which are different than making a prima facie case or the objection itself. Comparative juror arguments are very different in response to the state's reasons than simply making a prima facie case. And she didn't raise those.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: You don't think at that moment right there she -- she's not prepared to do that?
I mean, not at all, Your Honor. I mean, the very next page, on page 176 --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I don't know. He says there's no Batson violation per se. I don't know. I mean, that's where Judge Mills says perhaps she could have been more assertive. And I take that point, and that's why this is hard.

Well, I think -- and this would get back to, I think, you know, you -- you, I think, framed it correctly earlier, Justice Kavanaugh, where you said, you know, look, is it objectively unreasonable, is (d)(2) met? And I think the ways we know that are a number of them. First of all, Ms. Steiner speaks only from page 158 to 176 of the transcript. During that time, she at least five times inserts arguments or objections without any prompting by the trial court. There's this talk about are there pauses in the trial court? There are no indication of pauses in here. Yet, five separate times, in addition to all the arguments she makes, she inserts herself. I mean, that was the Batson objection. They didn't -- you know, there's no indication that the judge paused, looked at her, and, said, well, you make a Batson objection. She inserted that. She inserted the bench conference. I'd close the point by noting at page 176 that the judge then did allow her to state the composition of the jury, her assertions about the composition of the county. And, you know, so she -- she had an opportunity to add more, and that's all she added, was bare numbers. Then we look at the posttrial motion. Even when she had days and days, all she came up with -- and this was belatedly -- was the amended motion for a new trial, belatedly comes up with one sentence that points the judge to nothing about these comparisons.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, that's --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: But, General --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: -- in the course of -- go ahead.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I mean, I think you've made the point that she didn't do very well, you know, that she could have done a lot better than she did. But that's really not the question before us. The question is whether she's waived her objection. And three times, she's told by the court that the objection has been preserved. So you're right, General, she should have said a lot more stuff. She should have been more assertive. But the only question before us is, did she waive her objection when, three times, she's told by the court, your objection is in the record, I hear you.

And this is critical, Justice Kagan. The Mississippi Supreme Court did not hold that her objection was waived. It held that her pretext arguments were waived. It up -- it upheld the finding on that --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: That's slicing the baloney very thin. (Laughter.)
It's -- it's -- Justice Graves in dissent --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I'm sorry, General Stewart.
My apologies, Justice Kagan.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Here we are after the prosecutor has done all his here's my race-neutral reason, here's my race-neutral reason, and then the defense counsel says: I'm not persuaded, I need to -- you know, I need to say something about this, I still have an objection. Well, at that point, of course, she's objecting to the ultimate finding.
I mean, she's object --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: This is after the prosecutor has given all his race-neutral reasons, and she's still objecting. So what could she be objecting to at that point?
Oh, I agree --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: She must be objecting to the fact that either the race-neutral reasons aren't credible or they're -- you know, they're -- or they're -- they're pretextual. That's what she's objecting to.
But --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: There's no other way to read the context of this colloquy without saying that at that point she's objecting, she's saying what the prosecutor gave you wasn't enough.

I agree that she is maintaining her Batson objection, Your Honor. I don't agree about the comparative juror pretext arguments that she made no suggestion of making despite many opportunities to do so.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I think you're arguing this on the merits. I think you're saying she didn't say enough to allow the court to find for her. But that's not the question before us. The question before us is whether the -- the state supreme court was right when it said she waived her argument. She might not have presented a good argument, but she didn't waive her argument.

She -- and -- and, respectfully, Justice Kagan, the Mississippi Supreme Court didn't say she waived the argument writ large. It said she waived -- she waived the pretext arguments that she never presented to the trial judge. And that's critically different. Justice Graves in dissent, my friend -- my friend in his federal habeas petition, agreed that the Mississippi Supreme Court resolved the claim on the merits. It held that the Batson pretext arguments, the comparative juror arguments that she had never made to the trial judge, that's what she waived. That's what she failed to --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, can I just follow up on Justice Kagan's questions. After the prosecutor gives the asserted race-neutral reasons, what else could she be objecting to than that those were pretextual?
I mean, I -- I think what we -- I mean, she -- I think she's saying, like, I -- I believe that I've made my case. I mean --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: No, no, no. Answer my question. After the prosecutor has given the asserted race-neutral reasons, what else could she be objecting to other than that they were pretextual?
I -- I mean, I think she's -- are you talking about page 175, Justice Kavanaugh?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Exactly.
Okay. I think, there, she's just making sure that her objection is preserved in the record.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: What else that's after the asserted -- just answer my question -- after the prosecutor has given the asserted race-neutral reasons and she goes back to Batson, at that point, what else could she be objecting to other than that the asserted reasons were pretextual?

I mean, I think it's the ultimate conclusion the district judge reached or -- pardon me -- the trial judge reached, that they were -- that they were race-neutral, in fact, and she hadn't shown discrimination. I mean, I think that --- that's why I think she -- she uses the word "reserve." And I think she wants to make sure -- I mean, that's -- that's the 175. She says, I'd like to reserve my --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: And then she -- then that's the first sentence. The second sentence, "I don't want to let the paneling" "go by without having those objections" and then repeat myself. "I think you've already made those," says the judge, and they were race-neutral. Can I ask a separate distinct question, just one question, which is, in the course of that paragraph, the court says -- and this is now a (d)(1) question, okay?
Yes, Your Honor.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: The court says, the trial court, "all the reasons were race-neutral as to members that were struck by the district attorney's office, and so the court finds there to be no Batson violation." Is that a legally correct analysis of Batson?
It -- it is in that it means that he is finding the actual -- the reasons to be race-neutral in fact. Like, it is --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: But is that the end of the Batson analysis in your view?
I mean, if -- if he's finding them to be the actual reasons, the race-neutral reasons in fact, then -- then yes.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: No, no, if -- if they're -- if they're race-neutral, is that the end of the Batson analysis?
If -- if it's just -- if the question is just are they facially race-neutral, then that's step 2, Your Honor.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Right. And that's not the end of the Batson analysis, correct?
The -- whether there's a facial justification it's race-neutral is not the end of the Batson inquiry.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Thank you.
What -- what I'm --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: That's -- thank you.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: But whether in the end they are race-neutral is the question, right?
That's right, Your Honor.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: And as to what she was objecting to, if she wasn't tacitly raising a pretext argument, what she said on 176 is, "Allow us to state into the record there is one of 12 -- of 14 jurors -- are non-white, whereas this county is approximately, what, 40 percent?" What she's -- what she's saying is that the -- the racial makeup of the jury that was selected was so starkly different from the racial makeup of the county that that would be sufficient to find that there were Batson violations.
Right -- that's right, Your Honor. And, actually, in the cert petition at page 38, the Petitioner emphasized this point as being part of the Batson presentation.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Counsel, I don't know how that could be. She starts her colloquy in that section by saying, I want -- at -- at some point, the defense is going to want to reserve both its Batson objection and a straight for Tenth Amendment racial discrimination. That reference, I'm not -- I don't think it was on the Tenth Amendment. I think what she meant was the -- the earlier objection that they spent a lot of time in voir dire on, on the cross -- whether the jury pool was a representative body, correct? There had been two objections.
Two -- two objections there, Your Honor.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: All right. So she's talking about the cross-rep -- the representation argument and the Batson argument. On the Batson argument, the court starts with that and says: You have already made it in the record, so I'm of the opinion it is in the record. She says: I don't want to let the paneling of the jury go by without having those objections. And the court thinks, I think you already made those, and they are clear in the record for the reasons previously stated. He says: All the reasons were race-neutral, blah, blah, blah. And then, as to the other issue, the other issue is the jury pool issue, oh, I've already ruled based on prior rulings from this -- the United States Supreme Court and the State of Mississippi that jury selection was appropriate. That's -- that the jury itself, the pool, was appropriate. And those are noted for the record. It is then when she starts talking about the jury pool as a whole, that as a whole and not on the Batson question. So I'm not quite sure that you're fairly representing her use of that one example or their colloquy on that one example.

Let me cite you something that shows it is -- it is a fair representation. It's page 38 of the cert petition. That's Petitioner's filing where he ties that very exchange to his preservation of his Batson claim.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: But, counsel, I -- I think, in fairness, Justice Kavanaugh asked you what more could she have done or why wasn't she, you know, responding to or trying to say that there's pretext when she was talking about the Batson question. You pointed to this 40 percent issue that she talks about, the 12 of 14 jurors, but, as Justice Sotomayor points out, that discussion was in reference to the jury composition issue and not the Batson issue. So regardless of what was happening in the cert petition, I'm talking about what's going on in the trial record in the discussion that they were having. It looks as though the court resolved the Batson question by not giving her a chance to make any more arguments or say anything more about it, and then he says, the court, then as to the other issues, and he moves on to composition, and that's when she starts making statements about 12 of 14 jurors are non-white. So I think we have to be clear about what's actually happening in the record and not ascribe to her representations that actually don't fit.
Can I make -- make two quick responses to that, Justice Jackson? One is my friend conceded this morning that that point went to her trying to get to the -- the Batson claim itself. And also --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Okay. Well, that's just not what the -- what the transcript shows, so --
But, Your Honor, we're here on AEDPA relief, and the question is whether a reasonable fact finder could conclude this.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: No, I'm not talking about the question. I'm talking about what the court said they were talking about at that moment. He resolved the Batson issue and then he says: And then as to the other issues, and there were two issues, and the other issue was about jury composition, and that's the one that she responds to with the relevant data.
And, respectfully, I don't agree. He conceded otherwise, Your Honor, and --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Okay.

-- I would also add she did it without prompting. There was -- there was no, you know, would you like to say more? I mean, she said the more that she wanted to say. And the key thing is, even when she had that opportunity, she did not present the comparative juror argument.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I don't -- I don't think it helps to -- to -- to misrepresent what the record obviously shows. Let me ask you another question because it seems as though the Mississippi Supreme Court is trying to have it both ways with respect to the significance of her arguments related to pretext. Is -- is -- is it your position that the argument -- that her argument was so central that the failure to present it waives any obligation of the court to rule on whether the reasons that the state has given are race-neutral and, therefore, there's no Batson violation here because she didn't say anything about it or, as you interpret the record, that alleviates the court of any obligation to say, that's one thing that I think the Mississippi court is saying, but, on the other hand, they also say it isn't necessary for the court to give her a chance. So either it's central, in which case the court had to give her a chance, or it's not central, in which case the court had to rule on it, I think, in -- regardless. So which is it?
I'm not sure I'm completely following the question, Justice Jackson. What -- what I would say --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: What is the significance of her argument related to pretext? Is it so necessary that without it, the court is relieved of any obligation to continue to look at the facts and to actually make a finding, or is it not necessary, in which case it seems to me that the court needed to do that regardless of the fact that she didn't bring any argument about it?

Right. So I -- I think, when you're -- if you get past step 2, the -- the court has to make an ultimate finding on non-discrimination, but it does so in light of the parties' submissions. No -- no precedent of this Court requires the judge to consider matters, especially intricate competitive -- compare -- comparative juror arguments that are not presented to it. I mean, that's something this Court -- it's in light of the parties' submissions.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: And your view is that --

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Thank you. Justice Jackson?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I just wanted to -- and your view is that if the court has to do its obligation in light of the parties' evidence, the court does not have the obligation to turn to her and say, what is your evidence about this? The court doesn't have to solicit the evidence from this party or give her an opportunity to present it?

Well, it doesn't have to affirmatively do that. There's every indication that in the trial -- in the record here and a reasonable person could certainly read the record to allow multiple opportunities to present that. There's nothing supporting the idea that the trial judge cut her off or certainly nothing compelling that view of the record, Justice Jackson.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Thank -- thank you, counsel. Justice Thomas, anything further?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Yes. General Stewart, would you -- you were about to discuss the role of AEDPA in our review. Much of this is being discussed as though we're on de novo review. So would you discuss what AEDPA requires?

Sure, Your Honor. I think we've been very focused on the (d)(2) piece, so -- so I'll -- I'll lead with that. But there have been various discussions about, you know, could the record be read this way, are there pauses that allowed her to -- you know, to step in, did the trial judge actually turn to her and give her this opportunity. You know, I heard lack of clarity. All those things mean that the -- that the Petitioner can't be granted relief under (d)(2). The record has to compel a finding that the trial judge failed on some factual matter, and it just cannot possibly compel that finding. As I've emphasized, I mean, Petitioner himself took a very different view of the -- the record and he now says the view that he took is objectively unreasonable. And I think that goes for the legal matters too, Your Honor. There has to be something objectively unreasonable here. And the record can be read certainly either of two ways. That would be enough on clear error review, Anderson versus Bessemer City. It's certainly enough for the state under AEDPA. Thank you, Your Honor.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Justice Alito? Justice Sotomayor?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: You seem to be suggesting that the only way that we could overturn the Mississippi or honor AEDPA is if the district court had said to her: Sit down, counsel, you made your Batson challenge, period. Anything short of that, they couldn't err in finding a way -- a non-waiver -- a waiver?
I mean, given the entirety of this record, there's -- there's no other reasonable conclusion.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, no, no, no. I'm -- I'm saying your argument seems to be that only if the trial court said, counsel, sit down, Batson's been preserved, I don't want to hear anymore, that that's the only way that on AEDPA review we could say Mississippi made an unreasonable determination of fact?
I mean, again, given -- given this record, I think that you would need something like that.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Where have we ever said that a waiver has to be that explicit? Don't we infer it from evidence?
Well, I mean, even if that were true, Justice Sotomayor, this gets back to what I just --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, even if it's true, AEDPA and unreasonable doesn't mean that all interpretations of a record are correct. I'd like you to point me to one part of this record, one word by the court that says do you have something more on race neutrality?
But that's exactly the point, Justice Sotomayor. She has none of that. And she has multiple indications that she could have --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: No, the problem is --
-- she could have asserted --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: -- that she was never given an opportunity on this record.
And --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: The way the record -- well, we can go -- I'm not going to argue with you on this point. The record speaks for itself.
May I respond just briefly? I think I could say something helpful on this, Justice Sotomayor.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: No, no, no. I was going to ask one last question, okay, on the preservation issue -- not on the preservation issue, on the comparative jury analysis on appeal, the comparative jury analysis on appeal. In answer to Justice Barrett's question, appellate courts can do their own comparative juror analysis even if not preserved below, correct?
They can.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: That's what happened in Miller-El and Snyder. Do you believe the Mississippi Supreme Court says it cannot consider those arguments because of the waiver or that it's choosing not to consider them?
It's -- it's saying that in general it does not. It can exercise its discretion to do so. We know that --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: It could do so?
It could do so.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So is that a plain error standard? Because plain error is what federal courts use to review evidence that has not been presented -- an objection that has not been preserved below. Could it -- it would be plain error, correct?

I mean, that's what the -- that's what has been said in the case. I mean, Flowers versus State III, the Flowers case, I mean, what the Court said was, because the error in upholding the strike of Juror Pittman affects a substantial right, we apply the plain error rule to find a Batson violation occurred. So, I mean, we had the question --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So Mississippi has a similar plain error rule? It has discretion to overlook a waiver, correct?
It has discretion.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So, if the record is clear that there was a Batson violation -- and we can argue about each individual juror whether the record is clear or not -- I want you to make an assumption, if the record is clear that there was a Batson violation, would the Mississippi court have erred in failing to -- to conduct that review?
And the answer is no, certainly not under AEDPA.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: No, not under AEDPA? It's a constitutional violation in a case where the court below did not make an actual step 3 analysis. You're saying that it wouldn't have been error?
I mean, that's -- that's consistent with the waiver or forfeiture of constitutional objections generally and with jury objections in particular.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Oh, that -- that -- we apply plain error.

And -- but state courts don't necessarily have do that. They can do -- do pure discretion. They can do different approaches. Nothing in this Court's cases bar that, Justice Sotomayor. And, I mean, I would just emphasize that this is -- this is a rule that has been embraced by most federal courts of appeals, and it's one that was surely reasonably applied here.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Yes, because we apply plain error.
Some -- some do; some don't. And, again --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Yeah, you always have to apply plain error.
That's not --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Plain error is required by the Rules of Federal Procedure. If an objection has not been preserved, the court has to determine whether the error was harmless or -- or --
And I -- I'm sorry, Justice Sotomayor.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: -- whether the error was harmless.
May I -- may I respond to that one, Justice Sotomayor?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Yes.

I -- I come back to Ford versus Georgia, where the Court affirmed that state courts can adopt these timeliness rules. Perforce, those rules are going to block some claims, perhaps even some meritorious claims. And given that signal, it was surely reasonable to adopt this rule, which ultimately vindicates and enforces Batson itself and makes for better Batson rulings, as we --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Thank you, counsel.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Justice Kagan?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: General, I want to take you back to the conversation that you and I were having and that you were having with Justice Kavanaugh, which is just this question of waiver, because I do believe that, given the Mississippi Supreme Court decision, that's the only question before us. The question is not whether this defense counsel put enough in the record to actually prevail on a Batson claim. The question is instead whether the Mississippi Supreme Court got it really wrong when it said that she had waived her argument that there was a Batson violation. And, again, I'm just staring at this transcript, and I guess, as to that question, I don't really see the ambiguity in this transcript because this is coming after the fact of the prosecutor saying we had race-neutral reasons for all of them, and she says three times, I want to contest that. And the court says over and over, it's in the record, it's in the record, it's clear in the record. And when a court says that to you three times, I actually don't believe that it's, like, I'm not going to say what can you do? I think she could have done more. I think she could have said: Judge, really, like, I'm not moving on to anything else until I get this out. But, on the other hand, it's hardly ineffective assistance of counsel to make a different kind of choice, to say: I don't want to antagonize this judge. If he's insisting on moving on, I better move on. That probably was a wrong decision. I'll say that that definitely was a wrong decision. But that's not the question before us. The question before us is only whether she waived her objection. And how could she possibly have waived her claim that there was a Batson violation when she says it three times and the court says three times it's in the record, you've done it?

Okay. I appreciate that, Justice Kagan. I'd -- I'd -- I'd make two points. One is I really have to emphasize it's not a holding that she waived the objection or the claim. It's a holding that she waived the pretext arguments, and that's critically different.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: It's a -- I'm saying it's -- that what they said -- the pretext argument is just a way of establishing a Batson violation. So, if you keep on saying there's a Batson violation here, then you're saying there's something wrong with what the state has told you about their race-neutral justifications. And if you tell me that she had to use the word "pretext" in what she was saying, I'll tell you that's not the standard.

And what I'm saying, Your Honor, is that she had to give the judge a chance to rule on the comparative juror arguments that she later claimed were central to her argument. She did none of that. She didn't give the judge a chance to rule on it.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Okay. In terms of giving people a chance, the judge had every -- the judge is the judge. The judge has every chance in the world to rule on whatever she wants to do. The judge could have said: You know, okay, I'll put you to it. Show me what you got. So you don't have to give the judge a chance.
I mean, Judge, I -- I -- Justice Kagan, I think --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: And the judge said it's all in the record, it's all in the record, it's clear.

No, respectfully, he -- he didn't say that, Justice Kagan. He -- he agreed that the objection was in the record. And all she said was, I want to reserve the objection. And he said it's -- you know, that's what he gave her a signal to. What -- what I'd emphasize, Justice Kagan, is, I mean, look --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: You think that the judge thought that -- that she was only objecting in the same way she did at the very start of the -- of the inquiry, that she was just making, like, a prima facie case? I mean, obviously, the judge did not think that. The judge thought that she thought that there was a Batson violation, and she said -- and he said, enough, it's in the record.

And -- and here's -- here's the key point, Justice Kagan. Whenever my friend or any hypothetical needs to suggest the judge cut her -- cut her off, it always has to use words that are not in the transcript. And she referred not to pretext, not to the desire to make more arguments. She didn't say, you know, Your Honor, I didn't make some arguments that I would like to make, can I just take a moment to preserve those? And every indication of this record is that he would have allowed her to. I mean, he allowed her to make an extended argument challenging death qualifications even though she conceded it was doomed. I mean, she talked about carpool routes and juror medical issues and jurors being married to each other. When she wanted to say something, she did. And the judge heard her out and very often ruled for her. In this part of the transcript, just like when -- when the actual Batson challenges in step 2 and step 3 were occurring, she didn't say any of that and didn't give any indication, and she still didn't do so in her posttrial motions.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Thank you.
So I -- that's what I'd emphasize, Your Honor.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Thank you.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Justice Gorsuch?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Briefly, I hope. Should you lose, what is the appropriate remedy? Let's say you lose on the (d)(2), so there's an unreasonable determination of fact. I know you're going to want to fight the hypothetical, but please don't.
Very good. (Laughter.)

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Okay?
We --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: If this Court would find there's an unreasonable determination of fact, but under 2254(a), of course, we can only grant a writ if we find a violation of the Constitution. So there's obviously more work to be done after we decide the waiver issue. Can you explain how that's going to proceed?

I mean, I think, number one, there would need to be a showing of a substantive, I think, Batson violation, potentially, overcoming (e)(1), for example, in district court. If this -- if -- if -- if this Court or the lower courts were to think that that -- that law and justice were -- were shown in this case to warrant issuance of the writ, I mean, I think it would go back to the state courts. I mean, this -- this would depend if the Court finds a substantive Batson violation, I think --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, no, we're not -- we're likely -- assume we're not going to make that inquiry, that we're going to confine ourselves to what we spent the last two hours talking about, which is the waiver issue, okay, and we find an unreasonable determination on the waiver issue. What more does a federal court need to do?

Got it. I mean, I -- I think, as we've said in our papers, the possible remedy in that case when it goes back down the federal chain would be a writ that would require release if the Mississippi Supreme Court does not in a certain amount of time undertake whatever analysis this Court holds to be lacking. So, if that's do a new step 3 analysis in light of the relevant arguments, that would be the -- the measured remedy there. I think that would be consistent, for example, with what's appeared when, say, habeas is granted for -- on a question of whether a confession was voluntary. You don't necessarily need to do a retrial -- retrial. You just need to see if the confession was voluntary. If it is, things can stand. I think similarly here, Justice Gorsuch.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Justice Kavanaugh?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: A couple things. First, I agree with you that the court does not need to do anything at the point in the transcript we've been focused on, defense counsel had said, I withdraw my Batson objection or, having heard the asserted reasons, I have nothing on pretext. So I agree with you in that situation. But that's, obviously, as we've explored, not what I -- it looks like it happened here. You -- you've said that she could have jumped in again after that colloquy on 175 after she twice raises it. But, at the end of that, the district court says, "The court finds there to be no Batson violation." Now, again, as Justice Kagan said, could have jumped in, but, at that point, he said you've made the objections, you preserved them, and there's no Batson violation. Right?
Agree with that framing because, you know, again, made the objection, Your Honor. I think that's the critical thing.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Right. And then, for why -- there are two possibilities for why I think that it got truncated here, which we've all explored. One is that the district -- the trial judge had a misunderstanding of what Batson required, didn't understand the third step, and that's in that sentence that I read before. Well, all the reasons were race-neutral as to members and so there's no Batson violation. Right? So that's one possibility. The other possibility, and Judge Mills in the federal habeas district court alludes to this, because Judge Mills applies AEDPA, correct?
He says he does. I --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Right.
-- I agree with that. (Laughter.)

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Yeah. No, but he -- he articulates the AEDPA framework. He's a very experienced district judge, been a Mississippi Supreme Court justice. He says he's applying AEDPA unreasonable. And what he says happens is it stopped after two steps. Simply put, no state court, whether it be the majority in the Mississippi Supreme Court or the trial court, conducted a full three-step Batson inquiry. And then he explains what he thinks could have happened. He's generous to the trial court on this, I think. "The trial court, seemingly eager to proceed to the case itself, quickly deemed the reasons as race-neutral and moved on." "The trial court's actions, perhaps understandable and relatable to this court" -- speaking to Judge Mills, trying to show empathy, I think, for the burdens on a trial judge -- "are error nonetheless." So I think, you know, whether the trial judge misunderstood the third step or the trial judge was just, you know, rushing it along to try to keep things moving or whatever, it just never happened.
And --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: That's Judge Mills, again, applying AEDPA or at least articulating it, but I agree with Justice Thomas completely. We have to look through the -- the AEDPA standards here.

And -- and so I appreciate that, Justice Kavanaugh. To -- to take the -- the second bit first, I would come back to Petitioner's own words where he declared on direct appeal that the trial judge did decide step 3. And this is surely a fair reading of that record. That's page 484 of the transcript. And he, again, links that to the same parts of the transcript that we do in Footnote 4 on page 484.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Okay.

And I -- I -- I think that's quite important. I think it shows that it's not objectively unreasonable to find that the trial judge did conduct step 3 here. Could it have used better, more clear words? I think, you know, of -- of course, that's true, but what I think the judge was really doing was he wanted to be clear. I am finding these race-neutral in fact. I think that is what he was doing. That is surely a permissible view of the transcript. And, therefore, on clear error and, certainly, on AEDPA review, I think it is the compelled view in this case.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Last question. Sorry to prolong it. Obviously, focused on this, but the reason this matters is this is a -- a death penalty case, right, and -- and he was 17 when he committed the crime, and he did not, not that this is good, but he was not the shooter, correct?
That's right, Your Honor. I mean, not the fatal shooter, that's right.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Thank you.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Justice Barrett?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: General Stewart, I just want to understand your answer to Justice Gorsuch on remedy. So, if we think that the Mississippi Supreme Court was wrong on the forfeiture/waiver point, I don't understand how it gets back. You said something about it getting, you said this in your brief, something about it getting back to the Mississippi courts. Wouldn't the remedy be that we send it back down below for then the federal courts to analyze whether there was a Batson violation based on the comparative juror evidence?
I mean --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I just don't see the route of bouncing back. It's not direct review.
Well, I -- I guess what I'm -- so it would not be -- we didn't suggest remand to state court straight from --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Yeah.

-- this Court, certainly, Your Honor. I -- I think we're responding to the suggestion that the writ should issue here at all. I mean, my -- my friend has maintained that the writ should flat out issue ordering release or retrial. And our view is that if a federal district court is issuing the writ here, the most it can do is an order that would correct the actual violation, which, by hypothesis here, is not conducting a full step 3 analysis. And that could be something that is resolved by the state courts and would eliminate the constitutional violation.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So you're saying the district court shouldn't -- if -- if we sent it back down -- I agree, we did not grant cert on the Batson question, so that's not for us to decide. But, if we sent it back down, you don't think that the district court, you know, or -- or, frankly, the Fifth Circuit -- I mean, he said that the court has what it needs in the record to look at the comparative juror analysis. Why couldn't the federal courts make the Batson determination themselves?

I think that would also be an option. I mean, I think, if the -- if you sent it back down to the Fifth Circuit and said, hey, look, you know, you were wrong to find waiver, I mean, I think it would have everything it needs in the Fifth Circuit to just flat out rule on the Batson violation. As -- as we said, you obviously know the merits of our position, Your Honor, on that one.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Yeah, of course. Okay. Thank you.
Thank you, Your Honor.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Justice Jackson, anything further? Thank you, counsel.
Thank you, Your Honor.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Ms. Ferguson.

Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court: State and federal appellate courts routinely decline to consider claims, issues, and arguments that were not preserved in the trial court, consistent with historical tradition. The Batson context is a particularly important time to apply that rule. Whether a Batson violation has occurred is fundamentally a question of fact. Requiring parties to preserve their arguments that a prosecutor's stated reason is pretextual ensures that trial courts can consider all of the relevant information as they make the factual determination whether discrimination has occurred, and it allows prosecutors to explain their strikes and decisions not to strike when the reasons are top of mind. Justice is better served when these questions are aired before the jury is sworn, when any errors can be fixed, rather than through a cold record on appeal. The Mississippi Supreme Court did not unreasonably apply federal law or unreasonably determine the facts when it determined that Petitioner failed to preserve his Batson pretext arguments in the trial court. This Court should affirm. I welcome the Court's questions.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, Ms. Ferguson, would Petitioner have preserved this argument, the Batson arguments, if he had been in federal court?
No, Petitioner would not have, I think, preserved the arguments. The federal courts would apply plain error and consider those arguments under that standard.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: What do you do with the points we've been talking about on page 175, where the defense seems to be looking down the road for something that's going to happen, said at some point, I'm going to want to reserve these questions. And the judge does say: You know, you've -- you've already made those, they're clear in the record. In other words, his response, the judge's response to I'd like to reserve them is that you have.

Well, Mr. Chief Justice, I think that that was likely a demonstration by defense counsel that she wanted to say more. And she, in fact, did say more. And so that -- I'd like to respond to something that was of significant discussion during the state's argument, which is that reference on JA 176 to the statistics. And the fair cross-section requirement applies to the venire, not to the selected jury. So, when the defense counsel is referring to the number of black jurors who are on the selected jury, not on the venire, that necessarily is an argument in support of the Batson claim and -- and shouldn't be an argument in support of the fair cross-section claim because she's talking about the selected jury. And so I think the -- the suggestion that that was only about the fair cross-section claim and not about the Batson claim just doesn't make a ton of sense. And I think it shows that she was, in fact, given the opportunity to raise additional Batson arguments and she chose not to raise any -- any argument as to jurors.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So you're -- you're saying when she said, at some point, I'm going to want to reserve this, that that was the half page of the record later?

I -- I do think that that's when she took the opportunity. And she could have said, you know, if I may, Your Honor, I have additional arguments to make. She didn't do that either before she said I'm going to want to make or after she said I'm going to want to make.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: In the federal courts, they already have plain error review. And counsel for the state tells us that the state also has the discretion to consider a plain error, correct?
That's right, Your Honor.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: All right. So, if the juror comparison is clear from the record that there was a Batson error, that could be reviewed and should be reviewed by the Mississippi court. No?

Well, I think two points on that. One is, you know, just the existence of an error being plain is not sufficient to make mandatory plain error review. And so, under state law, the state court had discretion to consider that argument or not depending on the other prongs. And it --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: If the step 3 analysis was never done by the court, how could it not be an abuse of discretion to fail to have done -- done it by someone?
Well --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: It's a judicial obligation to do a step 3.
It is a judicial obligation for the court to engage in step 3, but I don't think it's an accurate depiction of the record to say that the trial court here did not make a step 3 finding.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I -- I know. We're going back and forth on that point.
And I -- I'd add one more response on that --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Thank you, counsel -- oh, go ahead.

I'd add one more response on that as to the existence of a step 3 finding here, and that's, on -- in this Court's decision in Purkett, the Court said that the state court had found at step 3 that the prosecutor was not motivated by discriminatory intent. And the -- the way the Court describes the facts in that case is that the state trial court, without explanation, overruled respondent's objection and empaneled the jury. So I think that's very similar to what happened here. And the Court found that there was, in fact, a step 3 finding even though there was no explicit "I find the prosecutor's stated reasons to be credible."

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: How could there be a step 3 finding if usually that's evaluating whether the race-neutral reason is the true reason or whether instead it was pretext? If there has been no argument that it's been pretext, how could there be a step 3 analysis? That's Point 1. And then Point 2, Judge Mills, who evaluated this, the federal habeas court, flat-out said multiple times it ended at step 2.

Well, Your Honor, I don't think that Judge Mills was -- was right to say that it ended at step 2. And I -- I know you pointed out earlier the state court's line that all the reasons were race-neutral. I think that saying all the reasons were race-neutral, to Justice Alito's point, demonstrates that the trial court at least implicitly had found those to be the actual reasons. You don't have a situation where the trial court said the prosecutor stated race-neutral reasons and so we find there to be no Batson violation. That would look like a state court that was misunderstanding what Batson requires at step 3 if the -- if the state court said that only stating race-neutral reasons was sufficient. But, here, you had the -- the state court say all of the reasons were race-neutral. And I think that's enough, particularly given what this Court found in Purkett, to show that there was an implicit credibility finding there.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: What -- what -- what about the court saying all of the reasons were race-neutral and so the court finds there to be no Batson violation?

Justice Jackson, I think the answer is the same, and that's because, again, if the reasons are race-neutral, that implies that those are the actual reasons. And that's distinct from saying the prosecutor has stated --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: But isn't that collapsing 2 and 3? I mean, 2 is race-neutral reasons; 3 is are they pretextual. And we've said you aren't supposed to collapse those two. So your argument just did so by saying, if you have 2, then you've satisfied 3.
Justice Jackson, no, I don't think that that's our --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: You didn't just say that if they're race-neutral, then that means they are the real reasons?

I -- I think if the actual reasons are race-neutral, so not whether the stated reasons are race-neutral. If the prosecutor has merely stated race-neutral reasons and the trial court doesn't credit those -- those reasons, or if there's any reason to believe that those are not the real reasons that the prosecutor exercised the strikes, then you could have --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Isn't there also a more complex way of looking at this that Miller-El brings up, which is not reason by reason but sort of the -- the comparison, right? There's no indication here that this court did any sort of comparative work, which would have been what we would have expected from the district -- I mean from the defense counsel if given an opportunity, correct?
I think, certainly, you -- given what the -- what defense argued on appeal, you would have expected that.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Right. So, if -- if the comparison is also a part of the determination of pretext, how does this record indicate that the court did any of that kind of analysis?

Well, I don't think that there's any particular indication that the court was sua sponte considering arguments that weren't raised, but I think that when it comes down to the ultimate question, this Court has explained several times the ultimate question is whether the prosecutor or the -- the striking party was engaged in intentional discrimination. And, necessarily, if the judge finds that the reasons were race-neutral, then race-neutral reasons, in fact, being exercised is incompatible with a finding of intentional discrimination.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Can I ask you a broader question? And then I'm -- I'm done. The United States has entered this case as an amicus curiae, meaning that you did not have to be here. And, as Justice Kavanaugh pointed out, this case is a capital case involving the conviction of a defendant who was not the shooter, a felony murder scenario. And so I guess I'm trying to understand the United States' interest. Your -- your -- your brief doesn't really pay a lot of attention or devote a lot of time to defending the actual conviction. So what -- what is the principle that you are seeking to have upheld in this case in which it's clear that the defense counsel said several times, I have a Batson objection and tried to preserve it, and the court, if anything, misled her into believing that she had preserved it by saying it's in the record? Why is the United States interested in being involved in this case?

Well, Your Honor, the United States is a party in many trials, including many criminal trials, and is subjected to Batson objections and defends in Batson cases. And so I think our interest is in defending the right of courts of appeals to exercise their discretion to consider juror comparison arguments and -- and not as, I think, Petitioner, if I may, Your Honor --

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Sure.

Not as Petitioner argued in Petitioner's brief, although it seemed to -- to walk away from today, adopt a rule that appellate courts must consider juror comparison arguments when they are raised for the first time on appeal.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Thank you, counsel. Justice Thomas, anything further? Justice Alito? Justice Sotomayor? Justice Kagan?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Ms. Ferguson, I want to go back to what you were saying before, and I'll -- I'll grant you something. I'm going to assume your view that the judge here did not collapse stage 2 and stage 3 and the judge understood what he was doing and that the judge made a determination that there was no Batson violation, the determination that you would make at the end of the day, all right? In exchange for my assuming your view on that, I need you to assume my view on something else, which is that the defense counsel understood that that's the stage that they were in; in other words, that now they were talking about the ultimate Batson violation, and what she was objecting to was the finding of the ultimate Batson violation. So let's say that they were both on the same page. We understand that we're contesting the ultimate Batson violation. So, if you assume those two things and the court says there was no violation and the defense counsel says I object to that, I think there was a Batson violation, and he said I got that, I understand that, it's preserved, and she says I want to make an argument about this, and he says it's preserved, it's preserved, how could it not be preserved?

Well, Your Honor, I would -- I agree with the state that there's a distinction between observing -- preserving a claim and preserving particular arguments. And simply saying I disagree with the ultimate finding is not sufficient to preserve every possible pretext argument under the sun. And so I think there needed to be some form of even gesturing at juror comparisons. There was nothing in the record at all until after trial to suggest that Petitioner's counsel thought that there was a problem with white jurors not being struck who shared characteristics with the black jurors who were struck.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So you think in the -- in the face of the court saying again and again, it's in the record, I got it, it's preserved, she has to make clear what the particulars of her view is why exactly there is a Batson violation?
In order to -- to preserve those particular pretext arguments for appeal, yes, under Mississippi law.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Thank you.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Justice Gorsuch?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: In fact, a lot of courts have issue preservation rules with respect to arguments, not just claims or issues.
That's correct, Your Honor.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: And we've never held those impermissible before?

No, Your Honor, and, in fact, this Court has repeatedly reaffirmed both in the context of Batson claims in state courts, in Batson and in Ford versus Georgia, the Court has reaffirmed that procedural rules are permissible, and then, in Singleton versus Wulff, this Court affirmed that courts of appeals in the federal system have discretion over when to accept unpreserved arguments on appeal.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Justice Kavanaugh? Justice Barrett?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Just one question, Ms. Ferguson. Is it unusual for the United States to appear as an amicus when we have a constitutional question before us that affects the United States in litigation?
No, Your Honor. It's quite common for us to appear.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Thank you.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Justice Jackson? Thank you, counsel. Rebuttal, Mr. Perkovich.

Just a few quick points. First, I want to address the -- the issue with may not in the Woodward case that constrained on direct review the inquiry. And that's simply the point. At that gateway issue, there was an understanding that they clearly may and this Court has done so routinely. So that's our fundamental point on that. With respect to the procedural sort of rules that Ford versus Georgia endorse as a basic principle, we have no qualm with that. That is a timely objection rule. Of course, that's not applicable here. And -- and with respect to a waiver rule and forfeiture, however it's framed, the problem is that it's not implementing Batson in step 3. It's obstructing Batson in step 3. And that's the work that's occurring in this case and the problem with that rule. With respect to the conflation of race-neutral findings and step 3, there is a very big step between determining something's race-neutral and determining it is credible. And that's where the work of the court at a minimum, the trial judge, is required, whatever is being pressed by the opponent of the strike for the reasons I've pointed to and are -- are spoken to forcefully in Powers with regard to the other stakeholders and the broader stakes for our society with regard to the Equal Protection Clause in this context. With regard to remedy, Batson, of course, ushered in a prohibition of the discriminatory use of strikes in a way that improved upon Swain and provided a specific framework. And so, when that framework breaks down, as it did here, that's a structural error. And so this has to return to its prior posture, much the way the last time this Court found a (d)(2) violation in Miller-El, which is to the district court and for a judgment entered for the Petitioner.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Thank you, counsel. The case is submitted.
